newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs mull rate cut to kick-start economy.
newsitem.headline: Czechs mull rate cut to kick-start economy.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Saturday the government and central bank had been discussing a cut in interest rates as part of a package of moves to help jump-start the economy.
Klaus said after a meeting with business leaders that the planned package would be bigger than originally expected, but refused to elaborate. Details are expected to be announced on Wednesday.

Asked if a rate cut was one of the planned measures, Klaus said: "We have naturally spoken about the possibility on this theme with the central bank governor, the finance minister and others in the past two or three weeks."
The Czech crown and interbank money markets have been very volatile in the run-up to the measures, with many analysts predicting a rate cut.
On Thursday, Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said the Czech National Bank (CNB) and the government had agreed to coordinate their economic policies.

Klaus and other government ministers have recently been critical of the central bank's moves last June to tighten monetary policy, saying the resulting slowdown in inflation has not been worth the price of weaker economic growth.

The Czech constitution requires the central bank to remain independent, but government ministers can participate in CNB board meetings, and CNB Governor Josef Tosovsky routinely attends cabinet meetings.
Klaus said the measures adopted would affect monetary and budgetary policy, banking, privatisation and foreign trade.
Last June the central bank hiked its key discount rate by one full percentage point to 10.5 percent along with a series of steps to choke off money supply and ease inflationary pressures.
Inflation fell to an all-time low of 6.8 percent, year-on-year, in March.

The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as companies imported new technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom. But industrial and construction output have both declined for two consecutive months as the central bank moves continue to bite.
